extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, researchers, policymakers interested in hate speech, law, and content moderation
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize the definitions, legal tests, harms, history, and regulatory/technical responses to hate speech across jurisdictions and online platforms. Useful for understanding how speech is classified and when restrictions or moderation apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: No single, consistent definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Hate speech is a term with varied meaning and has no single, consistent definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes definitional ambiguity across jurisdictions and disciplines; any evaluation must therefore specify which definitional standard is being applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cambridge Dictionary definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Hate speech = 'public speech that expresses hate or encourages violence towards a person or group based on something such as race, religion, sex, or sexual orientation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lexicographic definition highlights public expression, hatred/encouragement of violence, and protected characteristics as core elements to check for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encyclopedia/theoretical definition — animosity or disparagement toward group characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Hate speech usually thought to include communications of animosity or disparagement of an individual or a group on account of a group characteristic such as race, color, national origin, sex, disability, religion, or sexual orientation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating speech, look for content that expresses animosity or disparagement tied to listed group characteristics; this framing emphasizes the disparaging quality rather than only calls to violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incitement to violence or prejudicial actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many laws describe hate speech as speech, gestures, conduct, writing, or displays that incite violence or prejudicial actions against a group or individuals on the basis of group membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal thresholds often treat incitement to violence or action as a stronger ground for restriction/prosecution; evaluators should assess causal/intentional links between the speech and likely violent/prejudicial acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disparagement, intimidation, or humiliation targeting group membership
rubrics_metrics.description: The law may define hate speech as communications that disparage or intimidate a group or individuals based on their membership in the group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should consider whether speech aims to demean, intimidate, or degrade the dignity of a group even absent explicit calls for violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protected-group identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws and definitions often hinge on whether the target is a protected group identified by characteristics (race, religion, sex, sexual orientation, disability, national origin, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determining protection status is jurisdiction-specific; evaluators must check statutory or jurisprudential lists for the relevant legal regime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional variance and remedies (civil vs criminal)
rubrics_metrics.description: In some countries, a victim of hate speech may seek redress under civil law, criminal law, or both; other countries (e.g., the U.S.) generally treat hate speech as constitutionally protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review whether the jurisdiction provides civil remedies (damages, injunctions), criminal sanctions, or excludes regulation due to constitutional protections before deciding enforcement or response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of hate-speech laws: public order vs human dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws can be divided into those intended to preserve public order (higher threshold for enforcement) and those intended to protect human dignity (lower threshold and more frequent enforcement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should identify the legislative purpose to understand applicable thresholds and likely enforcement patterns; examples show dignity-based laws are enforced more often.

rubrics_metrics.name: International human-rights limits (ICCPR Articles 19(3) and 20(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 19(3) permits restrictions on freedom of expression when provided by law and necessary to protect rights/reputations of others or public order/health/morals; Article 20(2) prohibits national, religious, or racial hatred that incites violence, discrimination, or hostility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing legality under international human-rights law, check that restrictions are lawful, necessary, proportionate, and pursue legitimate aims; Article 20(2) specifically addresses prohibition of hate that incites harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: EU Framework Decision requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The EU Framework Decision 2008/913/JHA requires member states to criminalize certain forms and expressions of racism and xenophobia (implementation and interpretation vary by state).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In EU contexts, evaluate whether national laws implement the framework and how courts have interpreted elements like incitement, public dissemination, and protected characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incitement to genocide as extreme hate speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Incitement to genocide is an extreme form of hate speech and has been prosecuted in international courts (e.g., International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incitement to genocide triggers international criminal liability; evaluators should apply high evidentiary and contextual scrutiny and consider international jurisprudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: State‑sanctioned or official hate speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Some states and state actors have been described as spreading official hate speech or incitement to genocide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating speech by state actors, consider doctrines of state responsibility, domestic law prohibiting incitement, and international human-rights obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online platform moderation standards and commitments (EU code of conduct example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Major tech companies adopt terms of service often banning hate speech; under the 2016 EU code of conduct several companies agreed to review the majority of valid notifications for removal of illegal hate speech within 24 hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platform-moderation assessments should check provider TOS, specific commitments (e.g., 24-hour review targets), notice-and-takedown procedures, and transparency reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content-moderation techniques and tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques include user reporting, AI flagging, manual review by employees, and algorithmic adjustments (e.g., search ranking) to suppress hateful content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate moderation effectiveness by examining detection accuracy, speed, human-review quality, escalation processes, and impacts such as over/under‑removal or bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement variability and practical limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforcement of hate-speech laws varies widely (example: very few prosecutions under some public-order statutes), and cross-border internet jurisdictional issues make consistent enforcement difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical evaluation must account for resource constraints, jurisdictional reach, conflicting foreign laws, and differences between law on the books and enforcement in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critiques of hate-speech regulation (viewpoint discrimination, censorship risks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars and activists argue hate-speech laws can constitute viewpoint discrimination, be used to persecute minority viewpoints, or have chilling effects; others argue current laws can be arbitrary in categories protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy or legal assessments should weigh free-expression concerns, risk of misuse, and whether restrictions are narrowly tailored and non-discriminatory in application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential social and psychological harms
rubrics_metrics.description: Research links exposure to racial hate speech and online discrimination with poorer mental health outcomes (stress, anxiety, alienation), with stronger effects among Black, Asian, and other minoritized groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of harms should incorporate empirical findings on mental-health impacts, differential vulnerability of target groups, and how harms factor into legal or policy justifications for restriction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical and behavioral indicators (predictors of online hate activity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some research identifies psychological traits (e.g., high degree of psychopathy) as predictors of involvement in online hate activity; other tested factors show no significant predictive power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing interventions or assessments, consider empirical predictors to target prevention/rehabilitation efforts, but note limitations and contested findings in the literature.
